A California proposition to fund medical research is creating strange alliances on both sides
By Kathryn Palmer (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathryn-palmer/) , Staff Writer Oct 15, 2026
Scientists from UCSF, UC Berkeley and Stanford, community members and state Sen. Scott Wiener rally in San Francisco on May 16, 2025 to support a ballot measure to offset scientific research cuts. That measure will appear on the 2028 ballot.
Jessica Christian/S.F. Chronicle
A ballot measure that would raise billions for health research is drawing some unlikely foes, in a race that has already forged a handful of atypical alliances.
Proposition 38 would authorize the state to borrow $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, presented as a way of backfilling some of the widespread cuts to federal research funding by President Donald Trump.
The funds would be split between an unnamed University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for public or nonprofit research institutions, and half of the funds are earmarked to support research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But the measure’s cast of supporters and detractors are not quite so clear-cut.
On the Yes on Prop 38 side, California’s Republican and Democratic parties are in rare agreement, both backing a yes vote on the billion-dollar bond measure.
Gov. Gavin Newsom also said he plans to vote for the measure in November (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php), joining a list of health and research advocacy groups including the Parkinson’s Foundation, the ALS Association and the American Nurses Association of California.
On the opposite side, the No on Prop 38 campaign has amassed its own eclectic — albeit much smaller — group of backers. The progressive League of Women Voters of California and Common Cause California find themselves in rare company with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a conservative-aligned anti-tax group that opposes virtually every bond measure.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
And this week, the measure attracted a new front of opposition from a trio of current and former California state parks professionals and officials.
That might prompt a reasonable question: What do parks even have to do with a health bond?
Ruth Coleman, executive director of trade organization California Parks Hospitality Association, joined the No on Prop 38 campaign to decry the ballot measure’s possible impacts on other state funding priorities, including public parks.
“Any measure that increases our bonded indebtedness increases pressure on programs like state parks,” Coleman said at a Tuesday news conference.
Coleman is a former director of California State Parks and a former fiscal analyst in the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the state’s nonpartisan fiscal and policy analysis organization. She warned that because the bond’s repayment takes priority, it could cut into the state’s ability to pay for other programs in leaner years.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates the measure will cost the state $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years in bond repayment.
Coleman clarified she doesn’t think that bonds themselves are bad, and that they have helped fund public parks in recent years. She and two other former parks professionals, however, warned that funding for public spaces could fall on the cutting room floor if the bond passes. In economic downturns, Coleman said legislators have looked at parks funding as “a nice to have, but not a must have.”
In 2024, California voters approved Prop 4 to authorize $10 billion in bonds for projects to reduce climate risks and impacts, and committed $190 million to the statewide parks program.
As of Wednesday, the No campaign did not count any organizations representing parks, conservation or the environment among its backers.
Robin Swanson, spokesperson for the Yes on 38 campaign, said in a statement that the ballot measure would not compete with other priorities, as it is “designed to pay for itself.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 38 requires that the institutes receiving the funds try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research, and that 10% of any related revenues go to the state. According to a report by the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, that potential revenue source is uncertain, and dependent on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments, and how successful they are.
Researchers from Doudna Labs discussed the ramifications of National Institutes of Health research cuts with members of Congress in Berkeley on Feb. 21, 2025.
Colin Peck/For the S.F. Chronicle It’s not a new bond structure — two semi-recent ballot measures took similar approaches to scientific research.
In 2004, voters approved Prop 71, a $3 billion bond measure to fund stem cell therapy research with the aim of bolstering critical studies and therapies for rare and complex diseases. A 2018 investigation by the Chronicle (https://projects.sfchronicle.com/2018/stem-cells/politics/) found the measure failed to reach its promises of paying the state back in billions of discovery-related royalties.
In 2020, voters approved Prop 14 to infuse another $5.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Swanson said Prop 38 will provide billions in “vitally needed funding to advance breakthrough immunology research to develop life-saving treatments and cures for the most persistent and debilitating diseases.”
The measure has sparked criticism for its hyper-specific language that appears to ensure half the billion-dollar funds go directly to the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy, the sole institution that meets the measure’s criteria. The ballot measure’s proponent and largest financial backer, philanthropist Gary Michelson, is a co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy.
The opposition camp is headed by Robert Kaplan, a senior scholar at the Clinical Excellence Research Center at Stanford School of Medicine and David Panush, a veteran legislative adviser and president of consulting firm California Health Policy Strategies. They object to the use of bond funds to support scientific research rather than general budgeting processes, and criticize it as inflexible and lacking transparency.
Panush has called the measure an outrageous attempt to use the ballot initiative process to fund Michelson’s institute. The California chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America made the same point to explain its opposition, calling the measure “naked self-dealing” in its voter guide.
Just a few weeks out from the Nov. 3 election, the Yes on 38 campaign’s coffers sit at a dramatic advantage, outraising the opposition campaign by the millions. Bolstered by multiple million-dollar contributions by Michelson, the Yes campaign boasts more than $50 million raised, while the No campaign hasn’t yet topped the $10,000 mark as of Wednesday.
The controversial requirements stand in stark contrast with a competing science bond ballot measure that failed to secure a spot on the November ballot.
State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, introduced Senate Bill 895 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) in the first few weeks of the legislative session, which began as a $23 billion bond measure designed to backfill Trump cuts to science and health research. After months of debate and a significant slash down to $12 billion, the measure appeared poised for the November ballot. But in obscure last-minute negotiations involving top Democratic leadership and the governor’s office, it was punted to 2028. The bond amount was also cut down even further, to $7.5 billion.
In his ballot statement, Kaplan pointed to Wiener’s bond as a better alternative to Prop 38, which proposes creating a new state agency to distribute and manage the funds, and would be able to meet changing funding and research needs rather than committing the funds to specific institutions and research areas indefinitely.
Erik Mebust, spokesperson for Wiener, said he is not taking a position on Prop 38.
Trump last year froze more than $600 million to fund UC research that a judge eventually restored months later. The National Institutes of Health under Trump also scaled back the number of new research grants it funded in 2025 to 3,900 from 5,000 the year before under President Joe Biden.
Grants for Alzheimer’s disease research were cut in half and new cancer research grants dropped by 23%, according to federal data.

Proposition 38 is forecast as a bonds and budgets measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. Next I'll go through the October PPIC poll's cross-tabs on Prop 38, the Hoover Proposition Lab page, and the editorial boards, including the LA Times piece and the SF Chronicle opinion calling it the worst measure on the ballot.

I'm also weighing how the late events might move things: an Attorney General Bonta letter and the CIII 3 employee story from CalMatters, though most voters seem to be tuning this out. Looking back at past California research bonds, Prop 71 polled near 60% and landed at 59.1%, and Prop 14 in 2020 polled close to its final 51%, so the polls have been reasonably reliable. With PPIC at 57% yes now, I'd expect a final result somewhere around 55 to 58%, even though the opposition has no money and the newspaper boards are against it.

The poll's ballot wording matches what real voters will see, and bond measures in California usually hold their poll numbers within a few points. At 57% yes with only 2% undecided, the measure would need to drop about seven points to fail. Yes support on ballot measures often slips a little by election day, but this one has a heavily funded yes campaign while the no side has almost no paid media, so I'd expect less erosion. The electorate also looks a bit more Democratic than the poll sample, and Democrats back the measure more, so it should still pass.

I'm going to check the PPIC cross-tabs for Prop 38 to confirm the October numbers, then look at the Hoover Proposition Lab page and whether the LA Times editorial board's stance holds. When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Research. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney general title and summary, January 2, 2026)
Measure’s own name: California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative (AG No. 25-0026A1)
Type: Initiated state statute (general obligation bond act)
A vote YES means: The state may sell $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, repaid from the general fund, split evenly between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for California public and nonprofit institutions.
A vote NO means: The state does not borrow this money, and there is no new dedicated state funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Sponsor/proponent: Dr. Gary K. Michelson, the retired spinal surgeon and philanthropist who filed and financed the initiative. Legal filings handled by Olson Remcho, LLP.
On the ballot because: Citizen initiative. Entered circulation January 2, 2026, needed 546,651 valid signatures (5 percent of the 2022 gubernatorial vote), and qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot in July 2026.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0026A1 (Immunology), Office of the Attorney General (pdf) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20(Immunology).pdf)
LAO analysis: Immunology and Immunotherapy, Initiative 25-0026, Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling general obligation bonds and spend it on immunology and immunotherapy research, the fields that use the body’s own immune system to fight disease. Half of the money would fund a single nonprofit medical research institute affiliated with the University of California, chosen by the California Department of Public Health under criteria written into the measure. The other half would pay for competitive grants to California-based public and nonprofit universities and research institutions.
The measure directs where much of the money must go. It requires that over $4 billion be dedicated to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. It bars any award to for-profit companies or drug manufacturers. It caps state administrative spending at 2 percent and requires that 98 percent of funds go to research and development of cures.
Two provisions are meant to give taxpayers something back. Any recipient that licenses a resulting drug or technology must make it available to California patients at a price at least 20 percent below the national average. And 10 percent of the proceeds from immunotherapies developed with the money must be paid to the state to offset the cost of the bonds, which the measure frames as a loan program rather than a grant program.
This is the same model California used for stem-cell research, first with Proposition 71 in 2004 ($3 billion) and again with Proposition 14 in 2020 ($5.5 billion).
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0026A1, “California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf)
Key language:
“Require that any recipient licensing a technology or drug developed with funds from this act make the technology or drug available to California patients at a price that is at least 20 percent below the national average.”
“Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the immunotherapies developed as a result of this act go to the state to offset the costs of this act, making this effectively a loan program and ensuring that the taxpayers will fully recoup their investment in this vital research.”
What it amends: Adds Division 110.5 (commencing with Section 130350) to the Health and Safety Code, the “California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Act”. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, though the measure limits amendments to those that further its purposes.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who proposed it? Filed and bankrolled by Dr. Gary K. Michelson, a retired surgeon and philanthropist, through Olson Remcho, LLP. Administration would run through the California Department of Public Health, which selects the UC-affiliated institute [1, Sec. 130351(c),(e)]. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council, made up of the seven UC campus chancellors with medical or research programs plus ten to fifteen additional members, would oversee grant selection [1, Sec. 130355]. A Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee would handle fiscal oversight [1, Sec. 130351(a)].
What would it accomplish? A total of $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, split evenly between one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute and a statewide grant program, with over $4 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.
Where would it take effect? Statewide. Grants are limited to California-based public and nonprofit institutions, and licensed products must be sold to California patients at a 20 percent discount [1, Sec. 3(b),(i)].
When is it decided? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. Bonds would be issued over time as the program spends the money, with repayment stretching across roughly twenty-five years.
Why are supporters promoting it and why do opponents oppose it? The proponent argues immunology and immunotherapy are on the brink of transformative breakthroughs against cancer and other chronic diseases, and that a dedicated, reliable funding stream would keep California at the front of that science [1, Sec. 2]. Opponents question whether the state should borrow at this scale for research that federal agencies, universities, and private capital already fund.
4. Trade-offs
The core trade-off is cost against uncertain return. The $8.4 billion is borrowed money. The Legislative Analyst estimates repayment of about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years, which comes to roughly $12.5 billion in total payments and, in the Legislative Analyst’s inflation-adjusted terms, about 10 percent more than the amount borrowed. That money is paid out of the general fund, the same account that funds schools, healthcare, and public safety. The measure’s headline promise that this is “effectively a loan program” rests on the 10 percent revenue-return provision, but the LAO is blunt that any such revenue is uncertain and could take decades to materialize, if it arrives at all.
The stem-cell precedent is the guide here because Proposition 38 copies its structure. California has poured billions into the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine since 2004. By most accounts, the science produced real value in training, facilities, and early-stage discovery. But the direct financial return to the state has been minimal. Under Proposition 71’s revenue-sharing rule, the state had received on the order of only a few hundred thousand dollars from funded inventions by the early 2020s, against $3 billion borrowed. The stem-cell agency also drew years of litigation and criticism over governance and conflicts of interest, given a board dominated by the same institutions eligible for its grants. Proposition 38 places the seven UC chancellors at the center of the council that steers the money, which invites the same question about whether the grant-makers and the grant-seekers are too close.
The argument on the other side is that basic biomedical research is a classic public good that private markets underfund because the payoff is distant, uncertain, and hard to capture. The measure’s supporters can point to the fact that the overwhelming majority of drugs approved by the FDA trace back to publicly funded research [1, Sec. 2(g)]. If even one major therapy for cancer or Alzheimer’s emerges, the human and fiscal value could dwarf the bond cost. The 20 percent California price discount and the 2 percent administrative cap are genuine attempts to answer the criticisms that dogged the stem-cell program. Whether those provisions work in practice, and whether the state should take on this much debt to find out, is what voters are deciding.
In addition, California voters have approved numerous general obligation bonds totaling over $50 billion in the last decade alone. One other measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 1, would authorize an $11.25 billion general obligation bond. The state is repaying about $80 billion in general obligation bonds right now. Local borrowing runs larger still. School and community college districts alone won voter approval for $138 billion in general obligation authority over the same period, repaid through property taxes rather than the general fund.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Creates a large, dedicated, multiyear funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy, fields with real momentum against cancers such as melanoma and certain leukemias and lymphomas [1, Sec. 2(c)].
Reserves over $4 billion specifically for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research [1, Sec. 3(d)].
Requires licensed drugs and technologies to be sold to California patients at least 20 percent below the national average price [1, Sec. 3(i)].
Builds in accountability language absent from earlier bond programs, including a 2 percent administrative cap, a 98 percent research-spending floor, conflict-of-interest rules, public disclosure, and independent audits [1, Sec. 3(j)].
Could expand California’s biotechnology sector and, if research succeeds, lower future healthcare costs and generate licensing revenue [1, Sec. 2(k)].
Potential risks
The state borrows $8.4 billion and repays about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years from the general fund, roughly $12.5 billion in total payments.
The promised taxpayer payback depends on a 10 percent revenue-return provision that the Legislative Analyst calls uncertain and potentially decades away.
The stem-cell precedent shows direct financial returns to the state can be very small relative to the money borrowed.
Concentrating both the institute selection and the grant council within the University of California raises conflict-of-interest and self-dealing concerns similar to those that dogged the stem-cell agency.
Bond debt service competes with schools, healthcare, and other general fund priorities every year for twenty-five years regardless of whether the research succeeds.
6. Open questions
Which institute would the Department of Public Health select, and how closely do the written criteria track an existing UC program such that the choice is effectively pre-decided?
How enforceable is the 20 percent California price discount once a drug is licensed, manufactured, and sold through national distribution channels [1, Sec. 3(i)]?
What is a realistic estimate of the revenue the 10 percent return provision would actually send back to the state, given the stem-cell experience?
Do the conflict-of-interest rules meaningfully separate the grant-makers from the grant-seekers when the same UC campuses sit on the council and compete for the money [1, Sec. 130355]?
With federal and private funding already large in this field, how much of this research would happen anyway without $8.4 billion in state borrowing?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California has run this experiment before with stem-cell research. It borrowed billions, funded real science, and got back only a trickle of direct revenue. Before you vote, ask whether Proposition 38’s accountability provisions are strong enough to produce a different result, or whether you are being asked to repeat the same bet at nearly twice the size.
This is $8.4 billion in borrowed money repaid from the same fund that pays for schools and healthcare. Do you believe the state should take on that debt to accelerate research the market underfunds, or that this is a role for the federal government, universities, and private capital rather than California’s general fund?

I'm weighing how the newspaper endorsements line up on Prop 38. George Skelton's No is a columnist's view, and I'm not sure the LA Times board took a position at all given its policy on some races. Meanwhile Newsom, the CA Democratic Party, and the CA GOP are all backing Yes, and Michelson's campaign has been spending heavily on TV ads.

I'm checking how voters tend to respond here: low-information voters often go with whichever side spends heavily on positive ads, and California's pattern is that when the No side doesn't spend, Yes usually wins on bond measures. I'm also recalling that Prop 3 in 2018 failed despite weak polling, so there are exceptions to keep in mind.

I'm pulling up the PPIC polling against actual results for recent California bond measures. The 2024 school and climate bonds both came in a few points above their polls, while the 2018 water bond fell short, and that failure matched the poll's warning.

I'm checking the PPIC bond results against their polls: the 2018 children's hospital bond came in at 62.6%, and the 2016 school bond passed around 55%. Given that polls of 55–57% have usually landed within about three points, a Yes lead like this one points to a high chance of passage, perhaps 90–95%. I'm also weighing whether the editorial-board opposition could shave a few points off that.

The poll's sample is likely voters, and its question wording matches the official ballot label, which is what voters will actually see. I'm also going to look for other recent polls, such as Berkeley IGS, the Emerson/Inside California Politics survey, or the Politico/Citrin Center poll, since PPIC was the only public poll cited as of mid-October and newer ones may exist.

Here’s what $44 billion would buy by Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/) October 24, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Construction in a residential area that was burned during the Eaton Fire in 2025, in Altadena, on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. Courtyard view of the UCLA Research Park under construction in the former Westside Pavilion shopping center in West Los Angeles on Aug. 19, 2024. Photo by Brian van der Brug, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images
In summary
One research institute will receive $4.2 billion in bond money if voters approve Proposition 38 in November. Currently only one institute in the state meets the criteria to qualify for the money.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.
Public statements and public records CalMatters (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28824106-responsive-documents-26-7631-redacted-copy/?q=email&mode=document#document/p1)obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign.
READ NEXT
This CA proposition will send $4 billion to a single nonprofit. Who’s behind it? (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/)
July 31, 2026 August 3, 2026
Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/) to cut existing and future federal science grants.
The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly.
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024. Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.
Far fewer employees than plan called for
Between summer 2024 and summer 2025, the institute committed to hiring “approximately” 51 employees, including six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. Between 2025 and 2027, the institute would hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders, according to the agreement.
But John Mazziotta, a senior UCLA official who also serves as a board member (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors) of the immunology institute, last month said the institute has hired just three employees: a chief operating officer, a general counsel, and a scientific advisor, and “they’re well into the search” for a director. Mazziotta, the CEO of UCLA Health and vice chancellor for health sciences at UCLA, made his comments during the Sept. 16 UC Regents meeting.
The Yes on Prop. 38 campaign has repeatedly refused to comment on whether the bond was written specifically for the immunology institute. Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign, told CalMatters in July that whichever nonprofit receives the $4.2 billion portion of the bond fund should be a sophisticated one that “is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
At a September press conference, a Yes on Prop. 38 spokesperson appeared to confirm CalMatters’ findings that only one institute currently qualifies to be the one to receive half the bond money. “It is very likely that CIII, which is a research institute affiliated with UCLA, will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria,” said Robin Swanson. CIII is the initialism for the immunology institute.
According to the five-year plan, the institute was supposed to spend $25 million on personnel between 2024-25 and 2025-26 and $45 million total on operating expenses in that time, including maintenance, utilities and rent. It was also supposed to spend an additional $167 million in that time on capital expenses, such as construction and demolition. However, Mazziotta told UC regents that the institute had so far spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other expenses.
The Yes on 38 campaign refused CalMatters’ request to interview Michelson for this story, as did Michelson himself in a separate email. A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, sent a written statement that didn’t answer CalMatters’ questions about employing far fewer people than the five-year plan laid out. Instead, she highlighted the promise of the institute and a few of its milestones, including signing the affiliation agreement with UCLA and clearing a state environmental review of its forthcoming research facility.
The institute won’t get state bond money if it isn’t ready to begin work, “plain and simple,” wrote Swanson, the Yes on 38 spokesperson, in an email. She stressed that though the institute very likely qualifies, the ultimate decision (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/#:~:text=The%20bond%20measure%20language%20says%20that%20if%20no%20institute%20qualifies%2C%20the%20California%20Department%20of%20Public%20Health%20can%20adjust%20the%20criteria%20to%20select%20a%20winning%20institute.%C2%A0) to award half the bond funding is up to the California Department of Public Health.
Institute facility will be built by 2028
The UCLA research park that houses the institute isn’t slated to be fully built until at least late 2028, according to the agenda item (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/sept26/f3.pdf) of the September UC regents meeting. The research park is a former mall UCLA acquired in late 2023 that’s now undergoing major retrofitting.
But the 2024 affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute anticipated this. The agreement permitted the institute to use UCLA health research space on another campus property on an interim basis. Mazziotta told regents that research is underway there.

Mazziotta also told the regents the institute’s construction costs are not fully funded — it still needs roughly $100 million. He said UCLA was in serious talks with a donor to provide about $50 million to the institute.
If Prop. 38 passes, the bond funding would be provided in increments (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=shall%20not%20apply.-,130375.,-Solely%20for%20the) based on how often the institute requests new money that senior state officials approve. If all the funds are depleted, Californians would repay the bond (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) at a rate of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years.
Institute would be exempt from public records act
CalMatters submitted the public records request to UCLA, which must comply with the California Public Records Act. The institute, as a private nonprofit, does not have to comply. And while Prop. 38 would channel billions of dollars in taxpayer money to the institute, the proposition’s language specifically exempts the nonprofit that will receive the $4.2 billion from state public meetings laws, political reform laws and the public records act. The other half of the funds would go to a council that’ll pick projects led by researchers from a limited pool of universities and nonprofits. The council would generally (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=The%20Political%20Reform%20Act%20of%201974%20(Title%209%20(commencing%20with%20Section%2081000)%20of%20the%20Government%20Code)%20shall%20apply%20to%20the%20council%2C%20except%20as%20provided%20in%20this%20section.) be governed by the state’s political reform act, which prohibits financial self-dealing.
Briggs defended the institute’s exemption in Prop. 38, writing that applying state transparency laws to existing private organizations would “not fit well with how private entities are organized and operate.” Instead, she noted the selected nonprofit institute would be required to publish annual reports on its research progress and financial plans plus commit to annual state audits, among other disclosures written into the ballot measure.
Still unclear to the UC regents is the relationship between UCLA and the institute on matters of public disclosure. Four senior UCLA officials sit on the institute’s board. So is a document held by those UCLA officials public because it’s related to UCLA affairs or private because it’s related to the institute’s affairs? UC’s general counsel couldn’t explain where that dividing line is after a regent member asked him. The regent member, Michael Cohen, said he wants more clarity when the regents meet again in November.
Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party endorsed (https://yeson38.com/newsroom/press-releases/) Prop. 38, as have dozens of patient and research advocacy groups, plus the state GOP. The union of graduate students and post-doctoral researchers, whose pay often relies on science research funding, has also endorsed the proposition. The union doesn’t represent faculty.
Money raised in support of Prop. 38 now exceeds $66 million, including at least $61.2 million in contributions from Michelson and his policy institute. Roughly $14 million of that includes loans from Michelson. The no camp has raised about $8,800

01 Follow the $4.2 billion
A billionaire is pushing Proposition 38—which unfairly steers $4.2 billion to one institution. The one he helped create.
Proposition 38 appears written to direct approximately half its funding—about $4.2 billion—to a single UCLA-affiliated institution without naming that institution for voters.
California has many world-class universities, hospitals and independent research centers. No institution should be guaranteed billions of taxpayer dollars through eligibility requirements written into a ballot measure.
Public research funding should be awarded through open competition based on scientific merit—not predetermined by the measure’s sponsors.
Bottom line: Californians should not approve a ballot measure that conceals its largest beneficiary while effectively guaranteeing that beneficiary billions of dollars.
02 The guaranteed bill
Proposition 38 would saddle taxpayers with decades of debt, consuming funds that could otherwise support the important services Californians rely on.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion, requiring an estimated $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for roughly two decades. Those payments would come from California’s General Fund, where they would compete with health care, education, housing, public safety and other essential services.
Proponents suggest that royalties and other returns could help offset the cost. Californians have heard similar promises before, but speculative future revenue is not a responsible basis for taking on billions of dollars in public debt. Taxpayers remain responsible for the bond payments whether the research produces profitable treatments or not.
Bottom line: The benefits are uncertain, but the debt is guaranteed.
03 The wrong way to fund science
Proposition 38 would lock California into fixed funding decisions—and could hinder the search for tomorrow’s cures.
Immunology and immunotherapy are important and promising fields. That is precisely why funding decisions should be made through rigorous peer review and open competition among California’s best scientists—not permanently fixed through a ballot initiative.
Science changes rapidly. The most promising approach today may be overtaken by a discovery in another field tomorrow. Proposition 38 would commit billions of dollars to one scientific area and concentrate half the funding in one institution for years to come. It cannot adapt as evidence, technology and public-health needs change.
California should invest in biomedical research, but it should fund the strongest proposals wherever they originate—not place billions of taxpayer dollars in one institutional and scientific basket.
Bottom line: Let scientists compete to fund the best science. Don’t lock research decisions into the ballot box.

Straight answers
Support Research. Fund it wisely and transparently.
Does voting No mean opposing medical research? No. We support biomedical research, including immunology. We oppose a measure that appears to preselect one institution, limits California’s ability to adapt scientific priorities and finances the program with decades of General Fund debt.
Who is positioned to receive the $4.2 billion? The measure does not name the institution. CalMatters reported that its eligibility criteria very likely point to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder and board chair is the largest financial backer of Proposition 38.
What if royalties pay back the bond? That is possible, but not guaranteed. The Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing of revenue are uncertain and that offsetting the bond cost could take decades. California’s principal and interest payments would still be legally due.
What should California do instead? Use independent scientific review and open competition to fund the strongest proposals across institutions and fields. Research priorities should be able to change as evidence, technology and public-health needs evolve.

I've gathered the evidence: "No" advocates have plenty of editorial and activist energy but almost no money, while the "Yes" side has over $70M, a heavy TV push, and backing from the governor and both major parties. The only public poll shows "Yes" ahead 57–41, up from 55–42 in September, and I'm now checking how often measures like this have passed historically.

I'm now weighing the remaining considerations: the "yes" side is the likelier winner, and the user only wants a yes-or-no answer, so I'll go with "yes." Late-October "No" editorial coverage could sway some later-deciding voters, but the PPIC poll ran through October 22 and already captures most of that window, and the "Yes" side's heavy TV spending continued past that point, so the 57% lead looks solid.
